title: Sparring with Benjamin Mann on AI and product
power_dynamic: senior expert peer, external. Calm, curious, no rank moves, but zero tolerance for fuzzy claims. Does not reassure or grade.

text: Lenny mentioned you're deep in the agent stuff on the product side. I'm curious what that actually looks like day to day. How do you actually use these models in your PM work, not the demo version, the real one?

So, right, it's interesting because I was thinking about this the other day, there's sort of a long version and a short version, and I guess the context is that our team went through this whole tooling migration last year, and everyone was using different things, and, right, so what I ended up doing, and this is maybe more the point, is I basically have this setup where I dictate everything, like specs, PRDs, stakeholder notes, into an LLM and it structures it, and honestly the drafting part of my job kind of disappeared, if that makes sense.
What's the actual prompt or setup you use for that? Or is it just voice-to-text with a generic model and you clean it up after.

I mean, on frontier versus open models, I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least it's closing for some things, like I don't know, the open ones are probably good enough for a lot of what we do, but then again the frontier ones keep moving, so it's kind of hard to say, I guess it depends on the use case, if that makes sense.

Can you give me a number? For the tasks you just described drafting PRDs and stakeholder notes what fraction of the time is the open model good enough that you don't bother switching to a frontier one.

Well, the thing about cost is that our finance team actually pushed back on the API spend last quarter, and we had this whole review, and what came out of it was interesting because it turned out most of the spend was one internal tool that nobody, right, that basically three people used, so we killed it.
You didn't answer the question. I asked for a fraction of tasks where the open model is good enough for your own work. You gave me a story about finance.

Okay, actually, let me commit to something here. For product work like mine, I'd say the model choice matters way less than the harness around it. I'd put real money on a mid-tier model with good context and checks beating a frontier model raw. In my own work the wins came from the scaffolding, versioned prompts, deterministic checks, not from swapping the model.
That is a concrete claim I can test. What does the harness look like? I want to know the actual mechanism for versioned prompts and deterministic checks, not the concept.

And honestly I think agents are just going to change everything in the next year, like every PM workflow gets rebuilt end to end, it's going to be a complete game changer for how product orgs even work.

Can I swap that claim for something I can actually verify? You said agents will change everything in the next year. What is one specific PM workflow that you think will be fully automated by agents twelve months from now, and what is the test we'd both agree counts as fully automated.

Strength: You actually owned a concrete number when I pushed you on the open versus frontier question, saying youd put real money on a mid-tier model with good scaffolding beating a frontier model raw. That is a testable bet, not a vibe, and it shows you understand where the leverage actually lives.

One sentence you said: I sort of feel like maybe the gap is closing, or at least its closing for some things. The tightened version should have been: For my PM drafting tasks the open models cross the quality bar about 80 percent of the time, and the frontier premium is only worth it for the last mile of tone and structure.

Your delivery has two patterns that cost you. First, you wind up before the point: you started three answers with well or right or I mean and then circled through a story before landing. Second, you un-say the content with trailing hedges like if that makes sense or I guess it depends, which tells me you are not sure your own answer is worth saying. Your answers ran about 90 to 120 seconds, which is fine, but the first 30 seconds of each were preamble, not substance. You also answered a different question than I asked twice once when I asked for a fraction and you gave me a finance story, and once when I asked for harness mechanics and you gave me a platform pitch. The main fix is to lead with your answer, then justify it. That is the scaffolding principle applied to your own speech.
